units.translation: 29. Thracian Zone, flourishing: Zone is a mountainous place so called, and a city of the same name, as Nicander says (fr. 28 Schn.).
30. In rows they stand close-packed: they are in ranks and in order, dense.
18 ἐπήτριμοι, that is, successive, added at the end in A
31-34a. From Pieria: Pieria is a mountain of Thrace, where Orpheus spent his time. Herodorus says (31 fr. 43a J.) that Chiron advised Jason to take Orpheus along with the Argonauts.
19 ἡ in L : ἣ in P | 21 A adds at the end from sch. 23/25a: being a seer and foreseeing that they could pass the Sirens with Orpheus sailing along. cf. W 29
b. Such: namely, as we have said. Lg
c. Ruling over Bistonian: it is also written 'and ruling over Bistonians'. LmP
23 Βιστῶνι τε in L : Βιστωνίτας in P
35. On the spot: meaning immediately, at once. Lg
37-38a. Peiresiae: name of a city; like Erythrae and Peiresiae. Lg
b. Great Apidanus and divine: Apidanus and Enipeus are both rivers of Thessaly. The Phyllaean mountain is in Magnesia.
4 Μαγνησίας Dittrich proposed on account of Steph. Byz. s.v. Πειρεσία : Μακεδονίας
c. Peiresia is a region or city, near which was the Phylleian. P

40-41. And after them Larisa: He means Larisa in Thessaly, which Acrisius founded, and which was named after Larisa, daughter of Pelasgus, as Hellanicus says (4 fr. 91 J.). There are three Larisas: the oldest is the Argive one, which is the acropolis itself; the second is in the Pelasgian part of Thessaly, which Homer (B 738) calls Argissa, being near Gyrtone, which Apollonius now mentions; there is also one near Troy, which Homer (B 840f.) mentions: 'the tribes of Pelasgians, those who [dwelt in] Larisa'. Apollonius said that Polyphemus was the son of Elatus, but Socrates (fr. 10 M. IV 498) and Euphorion (fr. 87 Scheidw.) say he was the son of Poseidon. The Lapiths were named after Lapithes, son of Apollo and the nymph Stilbe.

45-47a. Nor indeed Iphiclus: Neither Homer nor Hesiod (fr. 50 Rz.2) nor Pherecydes (3 fr. 110 J.) say that Iphiclus sailed with the Argonauts. That Jason's mother was Alcimede, Pherecydes (3 fr. 104a J.) agrees with Apollonius. But Herodorus (31 fr. 40 J.) says that Polypheme, daughter of Autolycus, was Jason's mother.
